scenario: WIBTA for kicking my girlfriends older sister out of our apartment? | Apologies in advance. This is a really long story. I’ve lived with my girlfriend for 2 years. We moved to the apartment we are at now a year ago. We used to live with her sister and another couple. We’ll call my girlfriend L and her sister J. We moved because J would always have people over , and we wanted the privacy of no roommates. Once we moved, someone took our spot there. Fast forward from when we left (May 2018) to January 1st, 2020. J fucked her roommates over by not paying the rent for two months, as our landlords just accepted cash. For two months, she took the $3000 spent it on “bills” that her sister isn’t even sure about. After ruining her relationship with her roommates, She got the money from family to pay the rent off, and asked L and I to move in until the end of January. Her uncle would pick her up and she’d move out of state. She basically never asked the uncle to come get her, mentioned to L that she might just stay in New York. My girlfriend, who isn’t confrontational, never opposed her living with us for free. So J has been with us for about 4 months, no job, just contributing sometimes with cooking. She only comes here to sleep after she parties with her friends. Our house is essentially a hangover den. What makes matters worse is because of the current situation, the job she had a chance at has shut down. So shes not even looking for work. But that isn’t stopping her from going out every other night, to parties, where she doesn’t even think that if she was to get sick from being stupid, it would affect us as well. L wants her out, but is really conflicted because it’s her sister. I don’t think she’d be happy about me speaking to J about it, even though she also wants J out. I don’t want to seem like a dick, but it’s at the point where I might just take the risk of L being mad at me. I want my home back. I’ve been trying to get L to talk to her, but she just hates confrontation. I think I might just have to tell J if she doesn’t find a job to fund her getting her own place, she needs to to back to her mothers. WIBTA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I should kick my girlfriend's older sister out of our apartment. Let me start by laying out the situation as I understand it. We've been living together for two years, and we moved to our current apartment a year ago. The main reason we moved was because her sister, J, was always having people over, and we wanted more privacy without roommates. That worked out well until J ran into some financial trouble. She didn't pay rent for two months, which caused some issues with her roommates. Eventually, she got the money from her family to pay off the rent and asked us to let her move in with us until the end of January. Her uncle was supposed to pick her up and take her out of state, but it seems like she's not really planning to go. Instead, she's staying in New York. My girlfriend, L, isn't confrontational, so she didn't oppose J moving in for free. Now, J has been with us for about four months. She doesn't have a job and only sometimes helps with cooking. She comes home to sleep after partying with her friends, and our place has become a hangover den. Because of the current situation, the job J had a chance at has shut down, so she's not even looking for work. But that doesn't stop her from going out every other night to parties, which is concerning because if she gets sick from being reckless, it could affect us too. I want J out, but I'm really conflicted because it's her sister. I don't think L would be happy if I spoke to J about it, even though L also wants J out. I don't want to seem like a jerk, but it's gotten to the point where I might have to take the risk of L being mad at me. I want my home back. I've been trying to get L to talk to her, but she hates confrontation. I think I might just have to tell J that if she doesn't find a job to fund her getting her own place, she needs to go back to her mother's. So, the question is: Would I be within my rights to kick her out? (WIBTA) First, I need to consider the legal aspects. Do I have the right to ask someone to leave my apartment? Since it's our apartment, and I'm one of the tenants, I believe I have the right to determine who lives there. However, if J is on the lease, that might complicate things. But from what I understand, J isn't on the lease, so legally, I can ask her to leave. Next, the emotional aspect. J is L's sister, and L is conflicted about confronting her. I don't want to cause a rift between L and her sister, but I also need to protect my living environment. It's affecting our home life, and J's behavior is irresponsible, especially with the pandemic and her partying habits. I also need to think about the practical side. J isn't contributing financially, and her presence is causing stress and discomfort. She's not looking for a job, which means she's not planning to leave on her own. This is creating a cycle of dependency and tension in our home. I should also consider if there's any alternative to kicking her out. Maybe setting some boundaries, like requiring her to contribute financially or limit her partying. But from the situation, it seems like J isn't willing to change her behavior, so setting boundaries might not work. Another angle is the impact on L. She's not confrontational, so if I take action, she might be upset with me. But I also need to consider her well-being. If J's presence is causing stress, maybe L would appreciate me taking action, even if she's initially upset. I also need to think about the long-term consequences. If I kick J out, what happens to her? She might not have anywhere else to go, but she's been irresponsible with her finances and relationships. It might be a tough lesson for her, but it's necessary for our peace of mind. In summary, while it's difficult because it's L's sister, the situation is causing significant problems in our home. Legally, I have the right to ask her to leave, and emotionally, it's necessary for our well-being. I should probably take action, even if it means facing some conflict with L initially.
